body:

Conflict: open AND closed → reject.
Valid format does not prove a true fact.
explain: A requirement states desired observable behaviour. Validation checks acceptable input under a chosen policy. This model rejects open and closed together. A well-formed open value could still be stale or false in reality. Activity A in the guide asks learners to write a testable closed-room instruction. Explain that validation occurs before inference.

title: How conditions combine
body:
AND: every condition
OR: at least one, including both
NOT: reverse a known Boolean value
explain: Use A=true and B=false: A AND B=false; A OR B=true; NOT A=false. Clarify inclusive OR. Do not treat missing data as a known false value. Our application tracks missing support separately. Formal two-valued truth tables and the application’s incomplete knowledge concern different things.
task: 20 seconds: evaluate AND and OR when both inputs are true.
answer: Both expressions are true; inclusive OR permits both.

title: Two reasoning mistakes to avoid
body:
IF student THEN access
Access alone does not prove student.
No “open” fact does not prove “closed”.
explain: A visitor may have access through another rule. This is why the converse is not entailed. Separately, unknown availability is a lack of knowledge, not an observed closure. Keep these two distinctions clear: rule direction and information completeness. Backward chaining will seek support for a goal, not assume the converse.

title: Forward chaining starts with facts
body:

R1: quiet AND solo → suitable
R2: suitable AND open → recommend

Then match R2 and add recommend. Keep original facts and avoid re-adding a conclusion. Scan until nothing new follows. Rule numbers label rules, not priority. Video 01 03:44 and Video 02 show the same pattern in different domains.

title: Backward chaining starts with a goal
body:
Goal: recommend
R2 requires suitable AND open.
R1 supports suitable from quiet AND solo.
explain: Work from a goal to candidate rules, then check their premises against evidence. This does not establish the goal automatically. If open is missing, recommend remains unsupported. In larger systems track active goals to avoid cyclic reasoning. The same facts and rules can support the same conclusion through either strategy; the direction of investigation differs.

title: Debrief: identify the blocked condition
body:

B: suitable only; open is missing
C: no new fact; quiet is missing
explain: Trace A in two steps, B in one and C in zero. Open alone cannot establish suitable. Missing support does not establish the opposite conclusion. Follow with a transfer prompt: ticket AND gate_open implies may_enter. With ticket only, what is missing? Gate_open. The point is to reuse the reasoning pattern beyond room selection.
answer: A uses R1 then R2. B stops before R2. C stops before R1.

Transition: Continue to BFS uses a queue.

title: BFS uses a queue
body:
Remove S → [A, B]
Remove A → [B, G]
Remove B → [G, C]
Remove G → stop
explain: The first enqueued state is removed first. Parent links yield S→A→G. Removal order S,A,B,G is not a path because no edge connects A to B. Ask learners to point to the path on the previous graph. BFS finds a fewest-edge path under the stated assumptions; with equal action costs it is also least-cost.
answer: Visited removal order: S,A,B,G. Returned path: S→A→G.

Transition: Continue to Fewest actions is not always fastest.

title: Fewest actions is not always fastest
body:
BFS route: S → A → G
DFS via B: S → B → C → G
A route: 10 + 10 minutes
B route: 1 + 1 + 1 minutes
explain: DFS follows a branch deeply and does not generally guarantee a shortest path. Here BFS has two actions and DFS via B has three. Under the alternative travel times the B route is faster: three rather than twenty minutes. The earlier fewest-action result remains true; the equal-cost assumption has changed.
task: 20 seconds: which route is faster with these costs?
answer: B is faster at 3 minutes, even though it has more actions.

title: A need is not a room property
body:
Given: quiet, power, open_A, power_A
R4 adds needs_quiet_power.
R5 still needs quiet_A.
explain: Use a fresh case without quiet_A. Wanting quiet cannot supply the missing room property. Ask whether the room is quiet; do not conclude it is noisy. This is a useful learner task because it exposes a modelling error that simple successful examples can hide.
task: 25 seconds: should the system recommend Room A?
answer: Not from these rules and facts. Verify quiet_A first.

title: Explanations still need reliable inputs
body:
Yesterday: open_A supports recommend_A.
Today: closed_A replaces open_A.
Recompute from current inputs.
A trace cannot verify the real world.
explain: Positive forward chaining adds consequences; it does not automatically retract an old recommendation. Our program recomputes from supplied current inputs. A trace proves support within the chosen model, not that a room is open now. A learned noise estimator could supply uncertain evidence for explicit rules, but the uncertainty still needs handling.
